label: Chapter 1: A Settlement in the Marsh

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Every city has an origin story.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What's the one for Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It begins with mud. The river is called the Senne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a small, slow stream that once wandered across a wide, wet valley in the middle of what is now Belgium, splitting into channels and forming islands as it went.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So not a grand beginning.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not at all. But people have lived along the edges of that valley for a very long time.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Archaeologists have found traces of Iron Age settlers in the Brussels area, at a site called Champ Saint-Anne, in the neighborhood of Anderlecht.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Romans? Surely they turned up.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Roman farms and country houses were scattered across the surrounding countryside, but the Romans never built a real town on the spot.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After the Roman Empire faded, Frankish settlers moved in.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In that same field in Anderlecht, a Frankish cemetery with more than three hundred graves has been uncovered, dating from roughly the years five hundred to seven hundred.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So farmers and fighters, living in small villages on the dry ground above the river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exactly, in the new Frankish kingdom that would eventually grow into the empire of Charlemagne.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Now I know there's a legend coming.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I can feel it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There is. Tradition says that around the year five eighty, a holy man named Gaugericus, known in French as Saint Géry, who was bishop of Cambrai, built a small chapel on an island in the Senne.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And is that true?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians are cautious, because the sources are later and less certain.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it's a good candidate for the seed of the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the place is still there. It's a square in the old center called Place Saint-Géry, with a former market hall standing close to where the island once was.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What about the name itself? Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In its earliest forms it appears as something like Bruocsella, and most scholars read it as meaning a home in the marsh, or a dwelling by the swamp.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's a very honest name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's the name a farmer would give to a wet piece of ground.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it tells us something true, which is that this was a settlement that had to deal with water.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So why did a town grow here at all, if it was a swamp?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Geography. The Senne valley sat on an important route.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Trade roads ran from the rich cloth-making cities of Flanders in the west to Cologne and the Rhine in the east.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Merchants carrying wool, cloth, wine, and metalwork passed through, and a place where a river could be crossed, or boats brought upstream, was a natural place to stop and do business.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the islands gave them safe ground.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Right, and the hills to the east offered a good spot for a fortress.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But for a long time it was still a small place in a much bigger political world.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Very much so. In the ninth century, Charlemagne's empire was divided among his heirs, and the region that would become Belgium found itself caught in the middle, in a long contested territory called Lotharingia, named for the Frankish king Lothar.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It went back and forth between the western and eastern halves of the old empire.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And who was actually in charge on the ground?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The dukes who ruled Lotharingia on behalf of the German emperors kept a loose grip, so local lords held most of the real power.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So when do we get a proper date?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the late tenth century. In the year nine seventy-seven, the German emperor Otto the Second gave the duchy of Lower Lotharingia, which is roughly today's Belgium and part of the Netherlands, to a man named Charles.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who was he?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A member of the old Carolingian family, a son of a French king and a brother of the reigning French king.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: An exile from the throne of France, looking for a power base.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within a couple of years, he built a fortification on one of the islands in the Senne, the same island with the old chapel.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that's the founding?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Something else mattered even more.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In about the year nine seventy-nine, Charles moved the relics of a saint named Gudula, a pious woman from the seventh century, to the chapel on the island.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Gudula became the patron saint of Brussels, and that move is the date most often given as the official founding of the city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I love the story about her. She went to church before dawn with a lantern.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the devil kept blowing out her light, and each time an angel lit it again.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Is there a caution coming?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Always. Modern historians point out that the story of Charles building a castle and founding the city rests on sources written long after the fact.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The real picture is probably messier, with a growing settlement, a chapel, a market, and local lords all developing over several generations.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But nine seventy-nine is the date that stuck, and Brussels celebrated its thousandth birthday in 1979.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Gudula's relics moved again, didn't they?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They did. In 1047, a powerful nobleman named Lambert the Second, Count of Leuven, which is a city about twenty-five kilometers to the east, moved them to a new church on a hill overlooking the valley.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He founded a college of priests there, called canons, to serve the church.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that church is the ancestor of the cathedral.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The hill church, dedicated to Saint Michael and in time to Saint Gudula as well, is the origin of the twin-towered cathedral that still stands in Brussels today.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Saint Michael, the dragon slayer, became the other patron of the city, and he stands on top of the town hall, as we'll see.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So by this point the pieces are in place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They are. A lowland market settlement on the river where merchants and craftsmen gathered.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A church on the hill, with wealth and influence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A castle for protection. And a ruling family, the counts of Leuven, who increasingly saw this place as an important part of their growing territory.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the walls?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Around the year eleven hundred, the people of Brussels built their first defensive wall, a modest circuit around the main settlement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Inside, the town was small, perhaps a few thousand people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They made cloth, baked bread, brewed beer, and traded.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Not a great city yet.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not yet. But a real town now, with walls, a market, a church, and a lord.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it was about to enter a time of rapid growth.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In the next chapter, the counts become dukes, and the craftsmen start flexing their muscles.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a muddy market square begins its transformation into one of the most famous squares in the world.
